title: Global Assessment of Urban Bike-Sharing Sensitivity and Resilience to Extreme Weather
items.abstract: <jats:p>As climate extremes intensify, assessing how bike-sharing systems respond and recover is vital for urban resilience. This study develops a comparative framework using a time-series Transformer model and scenario analysis to evaluate demand under extreme heat, cold, heavy rain, and snowfall, using hourly trip and weather data from 14 cities worldwide (2023–2025). The sensitivity analysis shows that extreme heat reduces demand by over 40% in hotter cities but remains stable in temperate ones, while extreme cold and snowfall cause the strongest suppression, often exceeding 80%. To capture resilience, we simulate recovery curves after rainfall and snowfall shocks: North American systems typically rebound within 6–7 hours, whereas Montreal and Seoul show more prolonged disruptions, while Oslo and New York recover faster with winter operations and flatter demand profiles. These findings highlight how climatic exposure and operational readiness shape resilience and provide evidence to support climate-adaptive management and long-term system planning.</jats:p>

title: Probabilistic Bike-Sharing Demand Forecasting under Changing Weather and Seasonal Regimes with Transformer-Based Models
items.abstract: <jats:p>Bike-sharing systems must plan fleet and rebalancing under changing weather and seasonal regimes. We conduct reproducible probabilistic one-hour-ahead demand forecasting on two public datasets (UCI Bike Sharing hourly data and Seoul Bike Sharing Demand) under forward-chaining temporal splits. We compare tree-based Random Forest and XGBoost quantile baselines with N-BEATS, a Transformer encoder, an Informer-lite encoder, and a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT). Across both cities, N-BEATS and tree models yield the lowest MAE, while TFT produces the best calibrated 80% prediction intervals (81.1% coverage in Seoul). Error and coverage degrade under extreme weather, motivating uncertainty-aware operations.</jats:p>

title: Explaining Station-Level Weather Sensitivity in Bike-Sharing Systems: A Spatial Analysis of Chicago's Divvy Network
items.abstract: <jats:p><span>Weather conditions are widely recognized as important determinants of bike-sharing demand. However, existing research has primarily focused on estimating average weather effects at the system, city, or user-group level, providing limited insight into why some stations are substantially more weather-sensitive than others. This study develops and applies a station-level Weather Sensitivity Index (WSI) to examine the spatial, built-environment, and socioeconomic determinants of weather sensitivity within Chicago’s Divvy bike-sharing system. The analysis proceeds in three stages. First, station-specific weather-response functions are estimated using three years of daily bike-sharing data and Negative Binomial regression models. Second, station-level responses to temperature, precipitation, snowfall, and wind are transformed into four dimensions of weather sensitivity and combined through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to construct a composite WSI. Third, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and spatial econometric models are employed to identify the factors associated with variation in weather sensitivity across stations. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity in station-level weather responses. Highly weather-sensitive stations are concentrated along Chicago’s lakefront and within recreational, tourism-oriented, and destination-focused environments, whereas stations located in more residential and activity-rich areas exhibit greater demand stability. Built-environment and socioeconomic characteristics explain a substantial share of observed variation in weather sensitivity. Stations located closer to Lake Michigan and within highly connected street networks tend to exhibit greater weather sensitivity, whereas higher activity density, larger shares of low-wage workers, and higher proportions of households owning multiple vehicles are associated with lower weather sensitivity. Spatial diagnostics reveal strong spatial clustering and significant spillover effects, indicating that weather sensitivity is influenced not only by local station characteristics but also by neighboring stations. The study contributes to the literature by shifting attention from average weather effects to variation in weather sensitivity, introducing a composite WSI, and demonstrating the importance of spatial processes in shaping weather-related vulnerability within urban bike-sharing systems. The findings provide practical guidance for targeted resilience planning and weather-responsive management of shared micromobility networks.</span></jats:p>
